core: The internal parts of a city and the central business district (CBD) as its commercial core
Classic internal-structure models of the North American city: concentric-zone (Burgess), sector (Hoyt), multiple-nuclei (Harris & Ullman), treated as generalizations with limits
The urban hierarchy: settlements ordered by size and function
The primate city and the rank-size rule
World/global cities as command points of the global economy (Sassen)

claims.claim: The central business district (CBD), commonly called downtown, is a city's commercial and services core, usually one of its oldest districts and the nodal point of transportation routes, and it carries the highest land values.

The concentric-zone model, idealized in the first half of the 20th century, organizes urban land in rings around the CBD; it is attributed to sociologist Ernest W. Burgess of the Chicago School (1925).

The sector model (Homer Hoyt, 1939) and the multiple-nuclei model (Chauncy Harris and Edward Ullman, 1945) were developed to explain where different socio-economic classes live within a city; the multiple-nuclei model treats the city as having several separate nodes rather than a single center.

These internal-structure models are generalizations with limits; contemporary metropolitan areas also show peripheral 'edge cities' and mixed suburban growth that the idealized ring model does not capture.

The rank-size rule describes a regular pattern in which the nth-largest city in a country is about 1/n the size of the largest city: the second-largest is about one-half, the third about one-third, and so on; the United States distribution closely follows it.

In some countries the largest city is disproportionately large relative to the second- and third-largest cities; these are primate cities (e.g., Buenos Aires is about ten times larger than Rosario, Argentina's second city). The concept of the 'law of the primate city' is attributed to Mark Jefferson (1939).

World (global) cities are metropolises closely integrated within the global economic system and playing key roles beyond their national boundaries; because of their financial markets and business services, London, New York, and Tokyo are dominant examples. The global-city concept is attributed to Saskia Sassen, who framed such cities as command-and-control centers of the global economy (The Global City, 1991).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the rank-size rule or primacy is the 'normal' city-size distribution.
positions: The rank-size rule describes a smooth distribution seen in large, economically complex, long-urbanized countries such as the United States.
Many countries instead show urban primacy, where one city dominates; a city can also be functionally dominant (high centrality) without being strictly primate.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are presented as empirical patterns, not laws; the lesson treats rank-size and primacy as two ends of a spectrum of national urban systems and dates/attributes the concepts.
